newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zairean envoys return home after talks in S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Zairean envoys return home after talks in S.Africa.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Thursday he was confident of a negotiated peace in Zaire, where a rebel alliance holds half the country and is demanding President Mobuto Seso Seko's resignation.

Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila and a government envoy flew home separately on Thursday after talks with South African officials, but Mandela said it was not clear if Mobutu was ready for direct peace talks.

"I have been speaking both to (rebel) president Kabila and to President Mobutu and as a result of the exchanges I have had with them and the other leaders in Africa, I am confident that a peaceful solution will be achieved," he said.
Mandela said Kabila was ready to meet Mobutu, but said he did not know what the beleagured Zairean leader would do.

"If President Mobutu wants to come we would welcome that," Mandela said. "I have spoken to him since last Saturday three times. He is very cooperative, but what he is going to do eventually I cannot predict. I believe he, himself, has an interest in a negotiated settlement."
Kabila arrived in a South African military jet on Wednesday and spent over an hour with Mandela. He flew back to Lubumbashi in Zaire on Thursday.
Mandela said Mobutu's envoy Honore Ngbanda simultaneously met Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and other South African government ministers. He also returned to Zaire on Thursday.
U.N. and Organisation of African Unity (OAU) special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun also held meetings with Ngbanda and Kabila during their stays in Cape Town.
South African officials have declined to comment on the substance or mood of Wednesday's proximity talks, but government sources said the outcome was "positive".
Another government source said Mandela was trying to steer the two sides toward a direct meeting and a settlement that included all factions claiming power or influence in Zaire.
"The important thing for the president is that nobody should be left out. He doesn't want one winner, he wants a coalition that leaves nobody on the outside," the source said.

Mandela praised Kabila for his willingness to negotiate after military advances have left him in control of half the country, including the richest mining areas and the second largest city, Lubumbashi.

"He doesn't want a military solution. He has made this clear over and over again. He wants a solution which will receive the support of President Mobutu and he has also made it clear that he has no intention of doing anything which will humilate President Mobutu," Mandela said.
Sources in the peace process said Mandela hoped to persuade Kabila to abandon his demand that Mobutu resign after 32 years in power before a ceasefire and negotiations.
Speaking before he left Zaire for Cape Town on Wednesday, Kabila took a hard line, saying: "There will be no ceasefire until Mobutu relinguishes power."

South Africa has not backed calls by the United States and some European governments for Mobutu's immediate resignation. Government sources said a peace that excluded Mobutu's followers would have little chance of success.

The Swiss government on Thursday rejected demands by Zairean rebels and Swiss politicians that it freeze billions of dollars Mobutu may have deposited. The cabinet said Mobutu was still head of state.
